{{improve categories|date=July 2024}}
In [[continuum mechanics]], a branch of mathematics, the '''Burnett equations''' are a set of higher-order continuum equations for non-equilibrium flows and the transition regimes where the [[Navier–Stokes equation]]s do not perform well.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://chempedia.info/page/181144203140177134020048169072027076118072084254/ | title=No text - Big Chemical Encyclopedia }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-fluid-mechanics/article/abs/burnett-equations-in-cylindrical-coordinates-and-their-solution-for-flow-in-a-microtube/F89FC9C029F70CC2669E61C6E5DB0A6B | doi=10.1017/jfm.2014.290 | title=The Burnett equations in cylindrical coordinates and their solution for flow in a microtube | date=2014 | last1=Singh | first1=Narendra | last2=Agrawal | first2=Amit | journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics | volume=751 | pages=121–141 | bibcode=2014JFM...751..121S | url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-10662-1_5 | doi=10.1007/978-3-030-10662-1_5 | chapter=Burnett Equations: Derivation and Analysis | title=Microscale Flow and Heat Transfer | series=Mechanical Engineering Series | date=2020 | last1=Agrawal | first1=Amit | last2=Kushwaha | first2=Hari Mohan | last3=Jadhav | first3=Ravi Sudam | pages=125–188 | isbn=978-3-030-10661-4 }}</ref>

They were derived by the English mathematician D. Burnett.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Distribution of Molecular Velocities and the Mean Motion in a Non-Uniform Gas|first1=D.|last1=Burnett|journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society |year=1936 |volume=s2-40|issue=1|pages=382–435|doi=10.1112/plms/s2-40.1.382}}</ref>

{{continuum mechanics}}

==Series expansion==

=== Series expansion approach ===
The series expansion technique used to derive the Burnett equations involves expanding the distribution function <math>
f</math> in the [[Boltzmann equation]] as a power series in the [[Knudsen number]] <math>\mathrm{Kn}</math>:


<math display="block">
f(r,c,t) = f^{(0)}(c|n,u,T) \left[1 + \mathrm{Kn} \phi^{(1)}(c|n,u,T) + \mathrm{Kn}^2 \phi^{(2)}(c|n,u,T) + \cdots \right]</math>Here, <math>f^{(0)}(c|n,u,T)</math> represents the [[Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution|Maxwell-Boltzmann equilibrium distribution function]], dependent on the [[number density]] <math>n</math>, [[Flow velocity|macroscopic velocity]] <math>u</math>, and temperature <math>T</math>. The terms <math>\phi^{(1)}, \phi^{(2)},\dots</math> are higher-order corrections that account for [[non-equilibrium effects]], with each subsequent term incorporating higher powers of the Knudsen number.

=== Derivation ===
The first-order term <math>f^{(1)}</math> in the expansion gives the [[Navier–Stokes equations|Navier-Stokes equations]], which include terms for viscosity and thermal conductivity. To obtain the Burnett equations, one must retain terms up to second order, corresponding to <math>\phi^{(2)}</math>. The Burnett equations include additional second-order derivatives of velocity, temperature, and density, representing more subtle effects of non-equilibrium gas dynamics.

The Burnett equations can be expressed as:

<math display="block">
\mathbf{u}_t + (\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla)\mathbf{u} + \nabla p = \nabla \cdot (\nu \nabla \mathbf{u}) + \text{higher-order terms}
</math>

Here, the "'''higher-order terms'''" involve second-order gradients of velocity and temperature, which are absent in the Navier-Stokes equations. These terms become significant in situations with high Knudsen numbers, where the assumptions of the Navier-Stokes framework break down.

==Extensions==
The Onsager-Burnett Equations, commonly referred to as OBurnett, which form a superset of the [[Navier-Stokes equations]] and are
second-order accurate for [[Knudsen number]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Shock Structures Using the OBurnett Equations in Combination with the Holian Conjecture|first1=Ravi Sudam|last1=Jadhav|first2=Amit|last2=Agrawal|date=December 23, 2021|journal=Fluids|volume=6|issue=12|pages=427|doi=10.3390/fluids6120427|bibcode=2021Fluid...6..427J |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1397256|title=Beyond Navier–Stokes: Burnett equations for flows in the continuum–transition regime|first1=Ramesh K.|last1=Agarwal|first2=Keon-Young|last2=Yun|first3=Ramesh|last3=Balakrishnan|date=October 1, 2001|journal=Physics of Fluids|volume=13|issue=10|pages=3061–3085 |doi=10.1063/1.1397256|bibcode=2001PhFl...13.3061A |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">
 \sqrt{\tau} \frac{du^s}{ds} - \frac{9}{8} \alpha_1 u^* {\left(\frac{du^*}{ds}\right)}^2 = \frac{\tau}{u^*} - \tau_0 -1 + u^*   
</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

{{NumBlk||<math display="block">
\frac{45}{16} \sqrt{\tau} \frac{d \tau}{ds} + \frac{9}{4} \gamma_1 \tau {\left(\frac{du^*}{ds}\right)}^2 -  \frac{9}{4} \Psi u^* \frac{d \tau}{ds} \frac{du^*}{ds} = \frac{3}{2} (\tau - \tau_0) - \frac{1}{2} {\left(1 - u^*\right)}^2 - \tau_0(1-u^*)
</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}
